problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A team of three data scientists forecasts weekly demand for 400 stores and 30,000 products, using nightly warehouse sales data plus promotions and public holidays. Eight-week forecasts must reach replenishment by Monday 06:00. The central IT warehouse cannot be changed.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

points.description: A managed, orchestrated ML pipeline performs ETL-based feature ingestion from traceable, immutably preserved sources, then prepares data, trains and evaluates candidate models offline, and governs artifacts, metadata, experiments, and versions end to end. Automated, environment-gated release workflows promote approved models to scheduled batch prediction deployments that write results to storage or analytics systems.

This system uses ETL to ingest traceable, immutable row-level features into an orchestrated, version-controlled ML pipeline running across managed services and pluggable execution engines. Commit-triggered automation builds and promotes releases, evaluates candidate models by a selected metric, and deploys scheduled batch scoring; the DataOps-centered toolchain may provide less comprehensive model-lifecycle automation than the other choices imply.

The system uses batch ETL to ingest row-level features, with manually script-driven analysis, preparation, training, validation, and deployment on a standalone managed cloud ML platform. Versioned artifacts are selected through offline evaluation, while unified release automation and broader lifecycle workflows automate packaging, release, and recurring operational tasks; manual execution may limit workflow automation during routine runs.

The system ingests traceable, immutable row-level features through batch ETL and runs them through managed, orchestrated pipelines for preparation, training, offline evaluation, and deployment, with reproducible lifecycle metadata and explicitly specified production dependencies. Environment-gated automation promotes selected models to scheduled batch prediction, while monitoring service health, data quality, shifts, dependencies, and model performance to support corrective action.

The system uses ETL to load row-level features into managed, orchestrated ML pipelines for preparation, training, metric-based candidate evaluation, and deployment, with reproducible lifecycle governance, immutable traceable data, and explicitly specified production dependencies. Automated lifecycle workflows promote releases through environment-specific validation and approval gates, then run scheduled batch predictions while monitoring service health, data quality, shifts, and model performance.

Description: An orchestrated, hybrid-engine ML pipeline ingests traceable, immutable row-level features through batch ETL, runs parallel candidate training, evaluates candidates by a selected metric, and versions pipeline definitions, artifacts, and experiments. Repository commits trigger staged build-and-release automation, while the selected model is deployed for scheduled batch prediction; the DataOps-centered composition may provide less complete model-lifecycle coverage.

The system uses ETL to load row-level features into managed, orchestrated ML pipelines for preparation, training, metric-based candidate evaluation, and deployment, with reproducible lifecycle governance, immutable traceable data, and explicitly specified production dependencies. Automated lifecycle workflows promote releases through environment-specific validation and approval gates, then run scheduled batch predictions while monitoring service health, data quality, shifts, and model performance.

This system ingests row-level features through batch ETL, then runs an orchestrated, reproducible ML pipeline on hybrid managed and pluggable execution infrastructure, with parallel candidate training and metric-based evaluation. Governed artifacts, immutable traceable data, explicit production dependencies, and environment-gated releases support scheduled batch deployment, while service-health, data-quality, and model monitoring inform operational oversight and adaptation.

This system uses ETL to load row-level features into an orchestrated ML pipeline running on a managed cloud ML platform, with explicit production dependencies and end-to-end versioning of data, artifacts, experiments, metadata, and model health. Metric-based evaluation selects candidates, while commit-triggered release automation promotes tested changes and scheduled batch deployments write predictions to storage or analytics systems; data remains traceable and preserved.

The system uses ETL to ingest row-level features, then runs orchestrated preparation, training, evaluation, and deployment workflows on a standalone managed cloud ML platform with explicit production dependencies and end-to-end artifact, experiment, and data governance. It compares candidates by selected validation metrics, promotes releases through environment-specific gates, performs scheduled batch scoring, and monitors service health, data quality, shifts, and model performance to support lifecycle automation and adaptation.

This system uses ETL to produce traceable, preserved features for an orchestrated ML pipeline running across managed services and selectable execution engines, with end-to-end artifact, dataset, experiment, and model governance. Commit-triggered automation builds and promotes reproducible environments and pipelines; metric-based evaluation gates scheduled batch prediction releases, while monitoring covers service health, data quality, shifts, and model performance.

The system uses ETL to load row-level features into an orchestrated, repeatable workflow on a standalone managed cloud ML platform, with explicit production dependencies and end-to-end lifecycle versioning. It evaluates candidate models by metrics, promotes them through environment-gated automation, and performs scheduled batch scoring, while preserving traceable immutable data and automating recurring lifecycle operations.

approaches.idea: What if a managed, pipeline-centered service carries the weekly batch lifecycle, with governed data and approval-gated releases?
What if pluggable managed engines make candidate comparison and future model changes more flexible?
What if a small team keeps the workflow script-driven on a single managed platform?
approaches.dropped_because: Manual workflow coordination conflicts with the one-week model-promotion target and does not provide a reliable automated weekly run.

approaches.idea: What if a simpler managed cloud platform provides reproducible model governance and automated candidate promotion without a hybrid engine stack?
approaches.dropped_because: The DataOps-centered composition does not automate the model promotion lifecycle required by Q2; changing to full lifecycle automation would abandon this approach’s defining scope.

approaches.idea: What if a single managed cloud ML platform supports an orchestrated, reproducible batch workflow with explicit approval-gated releases?

trajectory.hypothesis: Managed orchestration, preserved data and gated releases should meet repeatability, weekly batch delivery and candidate testing with little custom operations work.
trajectory.observation: The point combines batch serving, lifecycle traceability and an evaluation pipeline; its approval gate is promising, but it does not by itself prove the six-hour runtime or first-week local setup.

trajectory.hypothesis: Hybrid engines and metric-based comparison should help test new model ideas, while versioned experiments and staged releases support reproducibility and promotion.
trajectory.observation: The hybrid composition widens runtime choice and supports metric comparisons, but adds integration and lifecycle-management burden for a small team.

trajectory.hypothesis: Script-driven work on one managed service may keep ownership simple, but is expected to struggle with automated weekly runs and fast candidate promotion.
trajectory.observation: The point leaves analysis, training and deployment transitions manual; that conflicts with the one-week promotion target and cannot be repaired without replacing the approach's defining workflow choice.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add service and data-quality monitoring plus explicit production dependencies to the managed pipeline, improving failure visibility and ease of reproducing the production environment.
trajectory.observation: The new values give concrete monitoring and production-environment practices. Monitoring still does not establish a 15-minute alert target or atomic forecast publication.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keep the hybrid engine approach but replace the DataOps-centered toolchain with full lifecycle automation and monitoring, while testing commit-triggered staged release.
trajectory.observation: Full lifecycle automation addresses the narrow scope of the DataOps seed, but commit-triggered release makes the approval gate less explicit than the gated alternative.

trajectory.hypothesis: Explore parallel candidate training on hybrid engines to speed model comparisons and support the six-hour weekly window, while retaining versioned experiments.
trajectory.observation: The DataOps-centered toolchain narrows lifecycle management to data operations and does not cover the model promotion automation required by Q2. Fixing that would abandon this approach’s defining scope.

trajectory.hypothesis: Use metric-driven evaluation of multiple candidates instead of a generic offline evaluation pipeline to directly support comparisons against production on historical weeks.
trajectory.observation: Metric-based candidate evaluation makes the comparison requirement explicit while keeping the managed pipeline and operational controls. Six-hour completion still needs workload sizing outside the design space.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keep hybrid engine flexibility but replace thinner experiment tracking and DataOps-centered lifecycle management with complete governance, metric-based candidate evaluation, monitoring and approval-gated releases.
trajectory.observation: The stronger governance and approval-gated automation address reproducibility and promotion; hybrid infrastructure remains an operational cost for three scientists.

trajectory.hypothesis: Explore whether an orchestrated workflow on one managed cloud ML platform can retain reproducible governance and candidate evaluation while reducing integration burden.
trajectory.observation: The standalone service removes hybrid engine integration while retaining batch scoring and lifecycle governance; commit-triggered release leaves the approval gate less explicit.

trajectory.hypothesis: Swap pipeline-centered infrastructure for a standalone managed platform while retaining monitoring, governance and gated release to test whether lower integration burden improves local maintainability.
trajectory.observation: The simpler platform preserves the assessed lifecycle benefits, but no evidence shows a material improvement over pipeline-centered infrastructure; both remain viable infrastructure choices.

trajectory.hypothesis: Add parallel candidate training to the hybrid, governed option to improve historical model comparisons and reduce experiment turnaround time.
trajectory.observation: Parallelism supports more candidate comparisons, but its runtime and cost are unmeasured and hybrid execution remains harder for a small team to own. The earlier gated hybrid point remains stronger.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace commit-triggered release with environment-gated deployment on the standalone managed platform to make the required approval step explicit.
trajectory.observation: The gate improves alignment with the required approval process while keeping a single managed platform; this becomes the best point in the simpler-platform approach.

alternatives.name: Governed managed batch pipeline
alternatives.summary: Use a managed pipeline service for weekly batch forecasting, end-to-end run and data governance, metric-based candidate evaluation, operational monitoring and approval-gated releases.

choices.reason: Batch ETL reads from the existing warehouse without requiring a new ingestion platform.
Repeatable connected stages coordinate weekly forecasts, candidate evaluation and deployment.
Managed pipeline infrastructure reduces the operational platform work expected of a small team.
Governed versions of data, artifacts, experiments and runs support exact historical reruns and candidate comparisons.
Compare multiple candidates on a selected metric before promoting a winner.
Environment gates automate validation and promotion while preserving the required approval point.
Scheduled batch prediction matches the weekly replenishment cadence and avoids request-time scoring.
Automated lifecycle workflows reduce repeated manual coordination for the three-person team.
Preserving traceable source data supports reconstruction of the inputs to a historical run.
Service health and data quality monitoring give operators visibility into run health and input changes.
Declared production packages and resources make execution environments reproducible.

considered.reason: A simpler managed platform was tested, but it did not clearly improve on pipeline-centered infrastructure.

relations.note: Batch ingestion is specified before the orchestrated workflow.
Candidate evaluation is coordinated within the selected ML workflow.

alternatives.name: Hybrid candidate lab
alternatives.summary: Use managed and pluggable engines for historical model comparisons, with full lifecycle governance and scheduled batch release; accept extra integration work for the flexibility to specialize execution.

choices.reason: Batch ETL uses the warehouse's existing nightly data without changing central IT systems.
An orchestrated pipeline repeats weekly work and links candidate tests to deployment.
Pluggable engines permit specialized or parallel candidate execution when comparison load grows.
Complete lifecycle traceability supports comparable experiments and historical reconstruction.
A common metric compares candidates before promotion.
Stage gates automate promotion after candidate checks and approval.
Scheduled batch prediction fits weekly delivery to replenishment.
Lifecycle automation compensates for limited engineering capacity.
Immutable, traceable data improves reproducibility of older forecasts.
Operational and data quality signals expose failing or unhealthy runs.
Explicit runtime dependencies support repeatable production environments.

considered.reason: Parallel training may shorten candidate comparisons but its six-hour fit is unmeasured and it adds runtime complexity; this refinement did not improve the best point.
Commit-triggered release was tested, but its approval gate was less explicit than the selected environment-gated approach.

relations.note: The ETL ingestion decision precedes the orchestrated workflow.
Model evaluation is included in the orchestration decision.

alternatives.name: Single managed ML platform
alternatives.summary: Run an orchestrated, governed weekly forecast pipeline on a standalone managed cloud ML service, with metric comparisons, declared dependencies and scheduled batch predictions.

choices.reason: Batch ETL reads the existing warehouse and leaves it under central IT ownership.
Pipeline orchestration automates recurring forecast and evaluation stages.
A single managed platform limits platform integration and infrastructure ownership for the small team.
End-to-end lifecycle governance preserves the artifacts, data lineage and run context needed for replay.
Metric-driven candidate comparison informs promotion.
Environment-gated release automation makes the required approval point explicit while keeping promotion automated.
Scheduled batch prediction provides forecasts on the weekly cadence.
Lifecycle automation reduces the work required to operate recurring pipelines.
Preserved source data and provenance support historical replay.
Declared runtime packages and resources support reproducible deployment environments.

open.reason: The selected design point does not settle a monitoring approach; the design space does not express the required alert timing or atomic delivery guarantee.

relations.note: Batch ingestion is decided before orchestration.
Candidate evaluation is coordinated by the selected workflow.

adrs.title: Coordinate the weekly forecast as a pipeline
adrs.context: The team must repeatedly prepare data, train and compare models, and publish weekly forecasts while relying on an unchanged central warehouse and limited engineering support. A manually coordinated process is hard to repeat on schedule.

options.name: Batch ETL with orchestrated stages
pros: Uses the existing nightly batch feed.
Connects repeatable preparation, training, evaluation and deployment stages.
cons: Does not establish that a particular workload finishes inside six hours.
options.reason: All retained alternatives need a repeatable batch workflow; each checked point satisfies the required ingestion-before-coordination relation.

options.name: Manual script-driven workflow
cons: Manual transitions undermine weekly reliability and timely model promotion.
options.reason: Dropped because the workflow's manual coordination misses Q2.

adrs.title: Choose the workflow infrastructure
adrs.context: The forecast load and the six-hour window require dependable execution, while only three data scientists are available to own the system. More flexible execution infrastructure may add integration work.

options.name: Managed pipeline-centered infrastructure
pros: Provides managed pipeline components as the main workflow infrastructure.
Reduces infrastructure work for the team.
cons: Creates some platform coupling and still needs measured capacity planning.
options.reason: Best fit for a small team automating recurring pipelines.

options.name: Hybrid managed and pluggable engines
pros: Supports specialized runtimes and candidate execution choices.
cons: Increases integration complexity and operating burden.
options.reason: Keeps flexibility for teams that value engine choice enough to accept added ownership.

options.name: Standalone managed cloud ML platform
pros: Limits the number of platform components the team must operate.
cons: Provides less explicit pipeline-centered infrastructure than O1.
options.reason: A simpler managed service is a viable alternative when reducing integration burden is the priority.

adrs.title: Preserve forecast history and compare model candidates
adrs.context: Historical reruns require preserving both source data and the exact pipeline, artifacts and run context. New candidates must be compared on past data before promotion.

options.name: End-to-end governance with metric-driven comparison
pros: Links governed artifacts, experiments, runs and dataset versions.
Compares multiple candidates on a selected metric.
cons: Requires disciplined retention and a metric that reflects business outcomes.
options.reason: This combination directly supports historical reconstruction and candidate selection across all three alternatives.

options.name: Pipeline and experiment versions with offline evaluation
cons: Provides less complete lifecycle and run traceability than end-to-end governance.
options.reason: A useful seed, refined toward complete lifecycle governance and explicit multi-candidate metric comparison.

adrs.title: Automate promotion and deliver forecasts in a batch
adrs.context: Forecasts arrive on a weekly deadline and candidate models need a short path to production after evaluation and approval. Batch delivery matches the replenishment cadence, but no checked point can prove six-hour completion.

options.name: Environment-gated release and scheduled batch predictions
pros: Automates environment validation and promotion around an approval gate.
Computes predictions on a schedule and writes them to a destination.
cons: Does not itself guarantee atomic output publication or the precise Monday deadline.
options.reason: It best expresses the approval-gated promotion and weekly batch delivery needs.

options.name: Commit-triggered staged release and scheduled batch predictions
pros: Automates builds, tests, artifact promotion and deployment from repository changes.
Supports the weekly batch prediction pattern.
cons: The selected value is less explicit about environment approval gates.
options.reason: Retains automated delivery on a simpler managed platform, with a weaker expression of the approval gate.

adrs.title: Automate lifecycle operations and declare runtime dependencies
adrs.context: A small data science team must own repeated forecasting operations and enable a new colleague to reproduce execution. Lifecycle automation and declared production dependencies help, but do not fully specify a local development setup.

options.name: Automated lifecycle with monitored operations and declared dependencies
pros: Monitors service health, data quality and dependencies.
Declares production packages and runtime resources.
cons: Monitoring coverage does not set the 15-minute alert objective.
Production dependency declaration alone does not guarantee a local setup within one week.
options.reason: Combines operational visibility with repeatable production environments and lifecycle automation.

options.name: Automated lifecycle and explicit production dependencies
pros: Reduces routine operations and makes production dependencies explicit.
cons: Does not choose a monitoring practice for weekly runs.
options.reason: Keeps the simpler managed-platform option focused on automation and environment reproducibility.

unaddressed.note: Monitoring practices can support visibility, but the design space has no decision for a 15-minute failure alert objective or transactional, all-or-nothing publication of the weekly forecast. Those reliability guarantees need a separate delivery and alerting design.
